paragraph.text_eng: Nenabush! gave a dance. He called together all the kinds of birds — that is, ducks. As he made them dance, he sang: “All of you, close your eyes!”
Now, one of them danced by the doorway. They heard him cry out. That was when he was killing them.
“Be sure not to open your eyes!”

He was using one arm to beat the drum as he sang. The other arm he was using to kill them. Hell-Diver was dancing there by the door. Then at one time Hell-Diver peered from under his eyelids. He made a loud outcry: “He is killing us, I tell you! Nenabush is killing us!”
Then they all ran out of the place, as many as were still alive. Nenabush jumped to his feet. He gave Hell-Diver a couple of powerful kicks in the rump.

Then he set about building a fire, a big fire. He dug a pit in the sand for his fireplace. The fire made the sand very hot. Then he placed there all the ducks of various kinds, as many as he had killed. He buried them all in the sand to roast where he had made his big fire. It was on a high sandy bluff by a stream.

paragraph.text_eng: Then he lay down to sleep. He lay with his buttocks sticking out. He looked just the same on his buttocks. He had a face also on his buttocks.

After a while some Indians came by there in canoes. Then those Indians spoke to him. It was the one of him at the other end there whom the Indians addressed. They gave him red paint.

paragraph.text_eng: In time he woke up. He had just about done his cooking, he thought. Then he pulled out those birds’ legs. The birds were gone. He tried them all, one after the other. All of them were gone. So now they had all been stolen from him. He picked up a stick. He prodded about for them. It was plain that they had all been stolen from him.
Then he looked round behind. He saw that the other one was decked out with red face-paint.
“‘You keep watch,’ I told you. And now it turns out to be you who let me be robbed, who let the Indians rob us when we were going to eat. Now you will really learn a lesson.”
Then he again built up a big fire. He stood there strad-dling that fire with his rump. Then he was badly burnt. Soon there came a sound. “Sizzle, sizzle!” was the sound.

So now he was all burned to a crisp there at the rear. He had a face like a human being likewise there at the rear. Again he looked at that other. Indeed, he was all burnt.

paragraph.text_eng: Then he set out again, going along the bank of the stream. As he went along he scraped against bushes where he was burnt. He was all bloody. In time he went along to another place farther up from the water. He looked at himself once more. Now he was all well. He had only a small scar. Then he went uphill again. Then he went off and away.
He saw those bushes. They are all red.
“Little Red Willow you will be called.”

After a time he said also to those larger bushes: “You for your part will be called Big Red Willow. And these bushes here will be called Spotted Bark. When my aunts have a stomach-ache they will made a medicinal drink of them.”

paragraph.text_eng: The white people who cook cook many different things. They cook very well. The Indians are not like that. When the Indian cooks he builds his fire on the bare ground. He builds his fire out of doors. He puts meat on a spit. He sharpens sticks to a point. He puts the meat on there. It tastes as if it were fried. In the same way he puts fish on a spit. That is the way the Indian does his cooking. He builds the fire out of doors when he cooks. When he bakes potatoes he buries them. Bread, too, he bakes under the ashes. It tastes just as if it were baked in an oven. That is the way the Indian does when he cooks.

paragraph.text_eng: In the olden time they did not employ doctors. The Indi-ans themselves knew what it was when they were in any way ill. They all worked together at making medi-cine of various things. They all knew what ingredients to mix according to the nature of their illness.

Also when one had a child there was a medicine for her to drink. They knew what would be good for that woman. They got well very quickly when they drank it. They remained sitting still only for two days when they were ill from bearing a child, so good was the Indian’s medi-cine. One would give it to drink to one’s daughter or to one’s daughter-in-law.

I carried the child about all night when my daughter died. The child did not eat. The only thing she ate was oranges. I did try to nurse her, but I had no milk at all there in my breasts. Finally I gave up trying to give the breast. I could not manage to do it at all. Then I used the bottle. She broke many a one sucking at it. She had a hard struggle to remain alive. I worked very hard. “I hope she will live,” I thought when her mother died.

paragraph.text_eng: Today she is a very handsome young woman. She is not married. She is a very fine person. She is not bad or foolish. Also, she is a very good worker. She does clean-ing the way the white women do it. She is one-fourth white. She is a grown woman now. She is fat. She speaks Indian only a little. She has almost forgotten how to speak Indian. She is always going about here and there working for people. That is the way she lives.
Now there are only the two of them. Her elder sister is living. She is there on Sugar Island.

Her father died two years ago. He had a palsy in his leg and in his arm. He died in Newbury, the big hospital. He was buried at Hessel. The cemetery is very beautiful. One sees all the great lake there, so high up is the place. You can see St. Ignace Island. And you can see all of Mackinac Island. That is where one of his daughters 1s buried. He is buried right where she is. His wife is not buried there. She died a long time ago. His wife died twenty-three years before he did. Only two of his chil-dren are living now. paragraph.text_eng: That son-in-law of mine looked frightfully miserable, nothing but bones, that son-in-law of mine who had the palsy. Two of my sons-in-law are dead. That one son-in-law of mine was sick one week. He had a stroke. He was unable to speak. He merely turned his eyes to look. In vain all the doctors and the priests tried to help him. All that time I did not sleep. I took care of him until he died. He died at noon. It was five days when he died. It is seven years now since that son-in-law of mine died. Six of his children are alive, four boys, grown men now, and only two girls. One is dead. That makes seven of them in all. His wife has not married again. She works. The one who was the wife of that son-in-law of mine works in the same place where I work. She takes care of all her chil-dren.

paragraph.text_eng: The Hurons lay all along on the ground. The Ojibwas had killed them. So there on the ground they lay, one beside the other, the ones who had been killed. They spared only one from the killing. They sent him back home.
“Come again. Come in greater numbers.”

They cut off his ears. The Ojibwa cut off half his nose. They never came again. That is why the place is called Iroquois Woman Island. That is why it is called so, be-cause all of them were killed. They kept guard against their coming again.

That is why that Huron hates the Ottawa and Ojibwa: they joined together to kill them. Now when he sees an Ojibwa he wants to kill him, he hates him so. Long ago, to be sure, they died, those tribesmen of theirs who were killed. But just the same they still know it, those who are now children. They will never forget it. They will always know how they were dealt with by those Ojibwas and Ottawas. That is why they hate them.

paragraph.text_eng: Sometimes, when there is a very thick fog, in the end there is rain. Sometimes, when there is much fog, it is blown aloft. It rains for a long time. There is a storm. In the end it comes to the point where there is a bad tem-pest. Especially in the autumn there are storms. That is the time of big winds. The wind is very powerful.

Last fall I heard of a big boat being wrecked. A big gale blew for four days. The storm came from the south. A great south wind was blowing. Trees were blown down. People were greatly frightened. Many old houses were blown over. Also, in the newspaper there was the report that many men had died. They were the ones who had drowned in that boat. Like trees that are washed ashore they lay there on the beach. Those were the people who had lost their lives. That was when there was a great storm for four days. One man was not found, one who had been a stoker on that steamboat. I do not know whether® they found the big boat that was wrecked. It was wrecked on Lake Michigan last fall.

paragraph.text_eng: One young man came from the Sault. I knew his father. Last winter I saw that old man. He told me about it.

“My son who had died was brought here. He had a life-belt around him, but it did not do any good. So that was the way he died,” the old man narrated. He wept much. He is one of the white people. It had been his only son. That old man has great difficulty in walking. But now he is getting a lot of payment. He was always paying for papers. It is from this that that old man now gets money. I have not seen him since, and perhaps he may even have gone away. He is all alone. His wife is dead. There were only the two of them living, his son and he. I do not know where they may have gone. He is not so very old a man, but for some reason he suffers a great deal. For some reason he has a hard time walking.

paragraph.text_eng: Those baskets are of many shapes. They have various names according to their uses, the little ones and the big ones: tall hampers, baskets for buttons and thread — this kind has a cover — and the oblong basket, and bas-kets for paper. One stores away all kinds of things in small storage baskets. That is the name of the kind I have been making. Later on I shall make also some of those larger baskets so that you all may see them. There are too few of those black ash splints. I would have made all the different kinds I know, but I have not much black ash. There is only a little of it. Also, not all of it is good. Much of it is cut too small. It should be cut carefully to make it look well. It looks well only when it is cut right. That is the way they do who make baskets. Also they use grass along with it. It is called sweet grass. It is not plentiful everywhere. There is only a little of it growing. It has to be gathered and stored away in summer to be used during the winter. This sweet grass is used for trimming on baskets.

This morning I chased her up out of bed. I scolded her again.
“If you do that way again in the evening, I will spank you. If you do that again, gadding about like that, I will spank you. You were not told to go fooling around like that.”

She knows what I told her. She is not angry at me for having scolded her yesterday evening. In the morning I scolded her again. The reason she goes round with me is just this that she helps me to walk about. She is not a bad girl. This is what I was told: “Take good care of her as you go from place to place.”

paragraph.text_eng: Only a few people practise this rite there where I come from. It is there at the place to which I went, westward, that those people are, those Midew-men. My husband, too, practised that rite, but not I.

sentence.sent_text: Bebezhig eta go izhitwaawag imaa wenjibaayaan.
Iwidi gaa-izhaayaan ebangishimog mii sa iwidi ayaawaad agiw bemaadizijig midewininiwag.
Gaye wii niwiidigemaagan mii naasaab gaa-izhitwaad: niin gaa wii.

paragraph.text_eng: Once in a while those Midew-men come, as they go about holding dances. But they are not good. They are danger-ous. They use beads to shoot each other. If one’s bead does not come back, then it kills him. So dangerous are those Indians. They are over there, in Wisconsin.

sentence.sent_text: Gijiishpin bwaa-biskaabiinid aniw omiigisiman mii go nesigojin.
Mii iwid; ayaawaad ekoseg iwidi Wiskaansin.

paragraph.text_eng: I did not see them myself. I was warned against going there.

sentence.sent_text: Gaa wii dash ningii-waabamaasiig niin igo.

paragraph.text_eng: Those are the Indians who still hold to their own relig-ion, to their Indian way of life.

sentence.sent_text: Mii agiw Anishinaabeg geyaabi menjigonangig odizhitwaawiniwaa odanishinaabe-bimaadiziwiniwaa geyaabi.

paragraph.text_eng: That is all.
